..
Issued at 425 AM CDT Mon Jul 20 2026

Early this morning, the Northern Plains lie between an upper 
level high pressure centered over Utah/Colorado and a shortwave 
trough digging into southern Manitoba. A weak surface cold front
extends from northwest Minnesota to north central South Dakota.
The Manitoba shortwave will continue diving southeast toward 
the western Great Lakes today, driving a secondary but stronger 
cold front through the state from north to south this morning 
and afternoon. Latest guidance has sped up the timing of the 
front, which could limit high temperatures to a few degrees 
cooler than what is currently forecast. Still expecting mostly 
upper 70s/lower 80s north to around 90 south, with dewpoints 
mixing down into the 40s from southwest to far south central 
North Dakota. Windy conditions are expected in the post frontal 
environment with a strong isobaric gradient and mean mixing 
layer winds around 25-35 kts. This should reflect in northwest 
surface winds around 20-30 mph with gusts to 35-45 mph. The 
strongest winds throughout the day are expected north and east 
of the Missouri River, diminishing toward the southwest corner 
of the state. Relative humidity is forecast to fall to at least 
25 percent along and south of I-94 from Highway 83 to the 
Montana border, and closer to 20 percent along the Highway 12 
corridor. The strongest winds and lowest RH are not forecast to 
overlap greatly, but there is a portion of south central North 
Dakota from around Lake Oahe to Lake Tschida where high 
resolution guidance indicates 20-25 percent RH (with slightly 
cooler surface temperatures than the NBM) under a local maximum 
of 25-30 kt mean BL winds. We have therefore elected to issue a 
Red Flag Warning for Morton, Grant, Sioux, and Emmons Counties 
from noon to 9 PM CDT. All other areas south and west of the 
Missouri River, as well as from around Bismarck to Napoleon to 
Ashley, are likely to see near-critical fire weather conditions 
this afternoon and early evening. Elsewhere, higher humidity and
fuel moisture content preclude fire weather concerns for today.

A separate shortwave over the Canadian Rockies early this 
morning will eject toward the region by late afternoon. This may
provide enough forcing in combination with diurnal heating and 
deep cyclonic flow to generate scattered showers and isolated 
thunderstorms across northern North Dakota late this afternoon 
and evening. Severe weather is unlikely given MLCAPE no greater 
than 1000 J/kg and EL heights under 30 kft, but effective bulk 
shear could be quite strong at around 40-50 kts. The 00Z NSSL-
WRF and ARW actually do simulate some long UH tracks through 
central North Dakota during the early to mid evening. The 
complicating factor is that the strongest shear (south) and 
highest CAPE (north) are not forecast to greatly overlap. So 
will not message a severe potential at this time, but will 
mention that a few stronger storms could develop in central 
North Dakota late this afternoon and evening. 

Surface high pressure is forecast to extend from Alberta to 
North Dakota on Tuesday, providing a much cooler and quiet 
weather day. A few showers cannot be ruled out given the 
northwest flow aloft, but forecast CAPE is very low. Still 
anticipating highs in the mid 70s to mid 80s on Tuesday, but we 
begin warming back up as soon as Wednesday as deep troughing 
over the Great Lakes shifts eastward while upstream ridging 
becomes amplified over the Rockies. The heat dome is favored to 
shift back over the central CONUS by the end of the week, with 
the Northern Plains lying near the top of the ridge. NBM high 
temperature projections warm by a few to several degrees each 
day, culminating with a widespread 100 to 105 degree forecast on
Saturday. Ensemble mean 850 mb temperatures around 30 C would 
support this heat, but 500 mb heights are forecast to be just 
slightly lower than the extreme heat episode from earlier this 
month. NAEFS/ECMWF climatological percentiles of lower/mid level
heights and temperatures exceeding the 90th percentile but not 
approaching maxima support this next round of heat not being 
quite as extreme as the previous one, but it could still be 
impactful. Chances for thunderstorms remain very low from mid 
week through the weekend, but that could eventually change given
our forecast proximity to the top of the ridge and the 
preceding northwest flow that could feature a shortwave passage
or two.
